title: Me and others: how we are alike, and how we are different

summary.text: Give everyone at home a bit of jaggery and a bit of karela. Everyone gets the same food, but the faces they make are not the same. All people have the same body parts and need the same things: food, water, sleep and people who love them. Yet each of us looks, sounds and likes things in our own way. In this unit you find what you share with your family in a mirror, test who likes which taste, and practise being kind to people who are different from you.
summary.art: A family of four around a low table with small steel plates of jaggery, lime and karela, each person making a different face as they taste.

intro.hook: Stand in front of a mirror with a grown-up. Count your eyes, then theirs. Now look at your hair, and theirs. What is the same? What is not?
intro.text: Almost everyone has two eyes, one nose and one mouth. But your hair, your height and your voice are your own. Scientists who study people look at both: the ways we are similar and the ways we are different. In this unit you find out how much you share with others, and how much is only yours.
intro.art: A child and a grandmother side by side in a mirror, both pointing at their own noses and laughing.

outcomes: By the end I can say three ways I am similar to other people.
By the end I can say three ways I am different from someone at home.
By the end I can say what I like, and that other people may like different things.
By the end I can say, from my own taste test, that one food can taste different to different people.
By the end I can name a kind thing to do, and say how it helps someone.
By the end I can make a guess, test it, and say what I saw.

terms.meaning: Similar means alike in some way.
terms.example: You and your cousin are similar: you both have ten fingers and you both like mangoes.
terms.art: Two children holding up their hands side by side, ten fingers each.

terms.example: Your hair may be curly and your friend's hair straight. Your hair is different.
terms.art: Two girls back to back, one with curly hair and one with straight hair.

terms.meaning: Taste is how a food seems in your mouth: sweet, sour, salty or bitter. You taste with your tongue.
terms.example: Jaggery tastes sweet. Lime tastes sour. Karela tastes bitter.
terms.art: A child's open mouth with tongue out, and a piece of jaggery, half a lime and a slice of karela beside it.

terms.meaning: Being kind means doing something to help another person or animal, or to make them feel better.
terms.example: Sharing your crayons with a new friend is kind. Putting out water for a crow on a hot day is kind.
terms.art: A girl handing a box of crayons to another child at a table.

explanations.definition: All people have the same main body parts and need the same things to live: air, water, food, sleep and people who care for them.
explanations.description: Every person has a heart, a mouth and a nose. Almost everyone has two eyes, two ears, two arms and two legs. Every person breathes, eats, sleeps and grows. A baby in Kochi and a baby in Kolkata both cry when they are hungry. Humans are animals, so we share a lot with other animals too. A cat, a crow and a person all need water, food and sleep.
examples: Everyone in your family has a heart beating inside them.
Children all over India, and all over the world, love to play.
A puppy and a child both need food, water and someone to care for them.
explanations.context: This card is about the ways all people are alike.
explanations.art: A row of children from different parts of India, of different heights and colours, all holding up two hands.

explanations.definition: No two people are exactly the same. We differ in how we look, how we sound and what we like.
explanations.description: Some people are tall and some are short. Hair can be curly, wavy or straight. Skin comes in many shades of brown, from light to dark. You can tell one grown-up from another with your eyes shut, because each voice is its own. Even twins who look alike have different fingerprints. And each person likes different things: one loves rice and rasam, another loves luchi.
examples: You can know who is calling you just from their voice.
Two sisters can have different favourite colours.
The lines on your fingertips are not like anyone else's.
explanations.context: This card is about the ways each person is their own.
explanations.art: A close-up of five different fingertips side by side, each with a different pattern of lines.

explanations.definition: The same food can taste different to different people, because each person's tongue and body are a little different.
explanations.description: Your tongue is covered in tiny bumps. Inside them are taste buds, too small to see. They tell you if a food is sweet, sour, salty or bitter. Not everyone's taste buds are the same. Some people find bitter foods very bitter, and others hardly notice. Babies are born liking sweet things. Many grown-ups learn to like bitter foods, such as karela or coffee.
examples: Nearly everyone smiles at a bit of jaggery.
A child may make a face at karela while their grandmother loves karela.
Some people find raw lime pleasant, and some find it far too sour.
explanations.context: This card is about why the same food can taste different to two people. It goes with the taste test.
explanations.art: A tongue drawn big, with tiny bumps on it and a few taste buds shown as little round shapes inside one bump.

explanations.concept: Why do we like different foods?
explanations.description: Scientists agree that two things matter. One is the body you were born with. The other is what you have eaten since you were very small. They are still finding out how much each one counts.
examples: A child who has eaten idli every morning may love idli all their life.
Some families have several people who all find bitter foods very strong.

perspectives.explanation: Some people are born with tongues that sense bitter much more strongly. For them, a bitter food really is stronger.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study babies and food
perspectives.explanation: What a child eats again and again, from very small, they often come to like. Even foods the mother ate before the baby was born can matter.

explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists are still working on.
explanations.art: A small girl at a table with a plate of food, with a little drawing of a tongue on one side and a family eating together on the other.

explanations.definition: Being kind means helping someone, or doing something that makes them feel better.
explanations.description: When someone may like things differently from you, you can ask them. Asking 'Do you like this?' is kind. Saying 'Yuck!' about someone's food is not. People are not the only animals who are kind. Elephants touch and soothe another elephant who is upset. Rats in tests have opened a little door to free another rat who was shut in.
examples: Asking a new child to play with you.
Bringing water for a tired grown-up.
Waiting for a slower friend on a walk.
explanations.context: This card is about kindness, in people and in other animals.
explanations.art: A mother elephant touching a young elephant with her trunk, and beside them a girl putting an arm round a crying friend.

agreed.text: All people have the same main body parts and the same needs.
agreed.evidence: Doctors all over the world study the same heart, lungs and bones in every person. Every person needs air, water, food and sleep.

agreed.text: No two people are exactly alike.
agreed.evidence: No two people have ever been found with the same fingerprints, not even twins who look alike.

agreed.text: Newborn babies like sweet tastes and dislike bitter ones.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have put a drop of sweet water and a drop of bitter water on the tongues of babies only hours old. The babies relax at sweet and screw up their faces at bitter.

challenging.claim: If I love a food, everyone else should love the food too.
challenging.who: A very common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: When a food tastes good to us, the taste seems to be in the food itself.
challenging.against: In a taste test, people eating the very same food make different faces. Each person's tongue and body are a little different, and so is what they are used to eating.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake: that a taste is the same for everyone.

challenging.claim: People who look different from us must be very different inside.
challenging.who: An old idea that many people have held
challenging.for: We notice skin colour, hair and clothes first, because we can see them.
challenging.against: Inside, all people have the same heart, lungs, blood and bones. Scientists who read the genes of people from all over the world find that we share almost all of our genes.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that looking different means being different inside.

challenging.who: An idea many people once held
challenging.for: We can talk about kindness, and other animals cannot tell us what they feel.
challenging.against: In 2011, Inbal Ben-Ami Bartal and her team in the USA found that rats free other rats who are shut in a small tube. Given chocolate as well, many rats shared the chocolate with the rat they had freed. Elephants soothe other elephants who are upset. Many animals help each other.
challenging.context: This card is about whether other animals are kind too.

big_questions.q: When you and a grown-up eat the same mango, do you taste the same thing?
big_questions.hint: Think about the taste test. Did everyone pull the same face?

big_questions.q: If you could swap tongues with someone for one minute, what would you want to taste?
big_questions.hint: Think of a food that someone at home loves and you do not.

big_questions.q: What makes you you? Is it your face, your voice, what you like, or something else?
big_questions.hint: Your face and your likes change as you grow. What stays the same?

big_questions.q: Which is bigger: how alike people are, or how different they are?
big_questions.hint: Think of the mirror and the taste test. What did you find that was the same? What was different?

story.title: Bornali's Tiffin
story.note: Masor tenga is a real Assamese sour fish curry, often made with tomato or lime. Rasam is a Tamil soup, often sour with tamarind and tomato. Pavakkai is the Tamil name for karela, bitter gourd. Nila, Bornali, Kavya, Ammamma and Appa are made up.
text: Nila was six, and she lived in Chennai. There was a new girl in her class. Her name was Bornali. Her family had just moved from Guwahati, in Assam, far away in the north-east of India.
At lunch, Bornali sat next to Nila and opened her tiffin. Inside was rice and a red fish curry. A sharp, sour smell came out.
Nila's friend Kavya wrinkled her nose. 'Yuck,' said Kavya. 'That smells funny.'
Bornali shut her tiffin. She looked down at her lap and did not eat any more. Nila felt a heavy feeling in her tummy. She did not say anything, but she kept thinking about it all afternoon.

At home, Ammamma was in the kitchen. Ammamma was Nila's grandmother, her mother's mother. She was cooking pavakkai, which some people call karela. Nila did not like pavakkai at all. It was much too bitter.
Nila told Ammamma about Bornali and the tiffin. Ammamma listened and nodded. Then she said, 'Let us do a test. Call Appa.'

Ammamma put three tiny pieces of cooked pavakkai on a steel plate. Next to them she put three little lumps of jaggery. 'Everyone eats one piece of each,' she said. 'Then we show what we think. Thumbs up, thumbs sideways or thumbs down.'
First, the jaggery. Nila put it on her tongue. Sweet! Thumbs up. Appa: thumbs up. Ammamma: thumbs up.

Then the pavakkai. Nila chewed it and shivered. Thumbs down. Appa chewed slowly and held his thumb sideways. 'Not bad,' he said. Ammamma closed her eyes and smiled. Thumbs up. 'I love pavakkai,' she said. 'When I was little, I hated it too.'
Nila stared at the three thumbs. 'But it's the same pavakkai!' she said.
'It is,' said Ammamma. 'The same food went into three mouths. Is one of us wrong?'
Nila thought about it. 'No,' she said slowly. 'It just tastes different to each of us.'
'Yes,' said Ammamma. 'Every tongue is a little different. And every person has eaten different foods since they were small. Bornali's curry may smell funny to Kavya. To Bornali, it smells like home.'
The next day at lunch, Nila sat next to Bornali again. 'What is your curry called?' she asked. 'Can I smell it?'
Bornali looked up. She opened her tiffin a little. 'It's masor tenga,' she said. 'Tenga means sour. My Ma makes it with tomato and lime.'
Nila smelled it. Then she tried a tiny taste on the end of her spoon. It was sour, like the rasam that Ammamma made with tamarind and tomato. Nila loved rasam.
'It's sour like rasam!' said Nila. 'I like sour too!'
Bornali laughed for the first time that week. Then she tasted the sweet pongal from Nila's tiffin. 'Too sweet for me,' she said, 'but nice.'

Kavya was watching. 'Can I try some too?' she asked. Bornali gave her a tiny bit. Kavya made a face. 'Too sour!' she said. Then she added, 'Sorry I said yuck yesterday.' Bornali smiled. 'That's okay. Everyone likes different things.'
That evening, Nila told Ammamma everything. 'Bornali and I are different,' she said. 'She is from Assam, and I am from here. She likes fish, and I like pongal. But we both like sour.'
Ammamma smiled. 'That is how it is with people,' she said. 'Find the different things, and you will find the same things too.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: Nila sees that the same pavakkai tastes different to three people, and none of them is wrong. Asking Bornali about her food, instead of saying yuck, helps her find that she and Bornali are similar too.
ask: Why did Bornali shut her tiffin and stop eating?
Ammamma, Appa and Nila ate the same pavakkai. Why did they show different thumbs?
What did Nila find that she and Bornali both liked?
What kind thing did Nila do the next day?
art: A school lunch table in Chennai: a girl in plaits opening a steel tiffin of rice and red fish curry, another girl wrinkling her nose.
A grandmother in a cotton sari, a father and a girl at a kitchen counter, each holding up a thumb: up, sideways and down, with a steel plate of karela and jaggery in front of them.
Two girls side by side at school, one smelling the other's open tiffin and smiling.
Three girls sharing small tastes from their tiffins, one making a sour face and the others laughing.

games.title: Stand Up If…: who is like me?
games.players: 2 or more players. One person is the caller.
games.context: This is a moving game about being similar and different. The caller reads a card. Everyone it is true for stands up. Some cards make everyone stand, and some make only one or two stand.

items.f: Stand up if you have a nose.
items.b: Everyone stands: we are all similar here.

items.f: Stand up if you like mangoes.
items.b: Count who stands. Likes are different.

items.f: Stand up if you need to drink water.
items.b: Everyone stands: every person needs water.

items.f: Stand up if you have curly hair.
items.b: Count who stands. Hair is different.

items.f: Stand up if you sleep every night.
items.b: Everyone stands: every person needs sleep.

items.f: Stand up if you like karela.
items.b: Count who stands. Tastes are different.

items.f: Stand up if you have a heart beating inside you.
items.b: Everyone stands: every person has a heart.

items.f: Stand up if your favourite colour is blue.
items.b: Count who stands. Favourites are different.

items.f: Stand up if you were once a baby.
items.b: Everyone stands: every person was a baby once.

items.f: Stand up if you can whistle.
items.b: Count who stands. Not everyone can.

items.f: Stand up if you have a mouth.
items.b: Everyone stands: every person has a mouth.

items.f: Stand up if you like the rain.
items.b: Count who stands. Likes are different.

items.f: Stand up if you laugh when something is funny.
items.b: Everyone stands: people all over the world laugh.

items.f: Stand up if you are taller than the door handle.
items.b: Count who stands. Heights are different.

items.f: Stand up if you feel sad sometimes.
items.b: Everyone stands: every person feels sad sometimes.

items.f: Stand up if you like to sing.
items.b: Count who stands. Likes are different.

items.f: Stand up if you speak more than one language.
items.b: Count who stands. Many people in India do.

items.f: Stand up if you need food to grow.
items.b: Everyone stands: every person needs food.

items.f: Stand up if you were born in this city.
items.b: Count who stands. People come from many places.

items.f: Stand up if you like to be hugged.
items.b: Count who stands. Some people like hugs, some do not.

rules: A child who cannot read yet can be the caller, with a grown-up whispering each card to them first.
Mix the cards. The caller reads one card out loud.
Everyone the card is true for stands up. Everyone else sits.
The caller counts who is standing, then turns the card over and reads the back.
Put the card on the 'Everyone' pile if everyone stood, or on the 'Some' pile if only some stood.
At the end, look at the two piles. Which kind of card made everyone stand?

flow.do: 1. Mix the cards. 2. Make two places on the floor for piles: 'Everyone' and 'Some'.
flow.say: When I read a card, stand up if it is true for you. Let's see who is like you.
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Stand up if it is true for you.

flow.do: 1. Read each card. 2. Count who stands. 3. Put the card on the right pile.
flow.say: Stand up if you have a nose. Look, everyone is standing! Now, stand up if you like karela.
flow.kid: Stand up if it is true for you. Look who is standing with you.

ask.q: Who stood up with you for the mango card?
good: Amma and Paati stood up with me.
Only I stood up.

flow.do: Look at the two piles together and ask the check question.
flow.say: Look at the 'Everyone' pile. What kind of things are on it?
flow.kid: Look at the 'Everyone' pile. What is on it?

ask.q: What is the same about the cards that made everyone stand?
good: They are about our bodies and what we need, like water and sleep.
Everyone needs them.

check.q: Which card made everyone stand up?
options: Stand up if you like karela
Stand up if you need to drink water
Stand up if you have curly hair
check.why: Every person needs water, so everyone stood. Liking karela and having curly hair are different from person to person, so only some stood.

setup.art: A family in a living room, three people standing and one sitting, while a girl reads a card aloud.
setup.caption: 1. The caller reads a card. Stand up if it is true for you.

setup.art: Two piles of cards on the floor, labelled 'Everyone' and 'Some', with a child putting a card on one pile.
setup.caption: 2. Put each card on the 'Everyone' pile or the 'Some' pile.

games.title: Kind Hands: act out a kind thing
games.players: 2 to 4 players. With 2, one is the grown-up and one is the child, and you take turns.
games.context: This is an acting game about being kind. Each card shows someone who needs help or feels sad. The player acts out a kind thing to do.

items.f: A new girl sits alone at lunch.
items.b: You could sit with her and ask her name.

items.f: A little child drops their ice cream.
items.b: You could share yours, or give a hug.

items.f: A grandparent or a neighbour is carrying a heavy bag of vegetables.
items.b: You could carry one bag.

items.f: A friend falls down and cries.
items.b: You could help them up and ask, 'Are you hurt?'

items.f: It is very hot, and a crow sits on the balcony with an open beak.
items.b: You could ask a grown-up to put out a bowl of water.

items.f: A friend does not like the food you love.
items.b: You could say, 'That's okay, we like different things.'

items.f: A child at school talks in a way the others laugh at.
items.b: You could stand next to them and say, 'I like how you talk.'

items.f: A grown-up at home is tired after work.
items.b: You could bring them a glass of water.

items.f: Your friend cannot find their pencil.
items.b: You could lend them one of yours.

items.f: A child in a wheelchair wants to join your game.
items.b: You could change the game so everyone can play.

items.f: A small child at home is scared of the thunder.
items.b: You could sit close and hold their hand.

items.f: An ant is stuck in a drop of water on the table.
items.b: You could let the ant climb onto a scrap of paper and put her down somewhere dry.

rules: Mix the cards and put them face down.
On your turn, a grown-up reads you the front of a card.
Act out one kind thing you could do. You can use words, or just your hands and face.
The others guess what you are doing. Then read the back of the card for one more idea.
Everyone gets a turn. There is no winner: everyone who acts something kind gets a clap.

flow.do: 1. Mix the cards. 2. Read the first card to your child.
flow.say: A new girl sits alone at lunch. How do you think she feels? What could you do?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. How does the person feel?

ask.q: How do you think the new girl feels?
good: Lonely.
Sad, because she has no friends yet.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. 2. Read each card. 3. The player acts. 4. The others guess, then read the back.
flow.say: Show us your kind thing. We'll guess what you are doing.
flow.kid: Act out a kind thing. Let the others guess.

flow.do: Pick up the card about the food and ask the check question.
flow.say: Here is a tricky one. Your friend does not like the food you love. What would you say?
flow.kid: Your friend does not like your food. What will you say?

check.q: Your friend says your favourite dosa is not nice. What is the kind thing to say?
options: 'You are wrong. Dosa is the best!'
'That's okay. We like different things. What do you like?'
'I won't play with you.'
check.why: The same food can taste different to two people, so neither of you is wrong. Asking what they like is kind, and you may find something you both like.

setup.art: Twelve small cards on a table, each with a simple drawing: a girl alone at a lunch table, a dropped ice cream, a crow with an open beak.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up reads a card.

setup.art: A boy pretending to carry a heavy bag for his grandmother, while his sister guesses and claps.
setup.caption: 2. Act out a kind thing. The others guess.

experiments.title: Same Food, Different Faces: does everyone at home like the same tastes?
experiments.context: In this experiment everyone at home tastes the same three foods: jaggery, lime and karela. Each person shows a thumb for each food. You find out if everyone likes the same tastes.
experiments.question: If everyone at home tastes the same jaggery, the same lime and the same karela, will everyone like them the same?
experiments.predict: Guess first. For each person at home, will they show thumbs up, sideways or down for each food? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Everyone gets the same size of piece from the same jaggery, the same lime and the same karela. Everyone tastes with eyes closed and shows a thumb at the same moment, so nobody copies anyone else. Everyone sips water between foods.

materials.item: a lump of jaggery (gud, vellam), broken into small pieces
a lime, cut into small wedges by a grown-up (each child tastes only a small piece)
a raw karela (bitter gourd), cut into thin slices by a grown-up, or 3 methi seeds for each person if you have no karela
a small steel plate for each food
a glass of water for each person
a sheet of paper and a pencil, for the results table
a knife, for the grown-up

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the lime and the karela. Leave out any food that someone is allergic to or has been told not to eat. Only taste foods a grown-up has given you.

schedule.what: Make the table. Guess the thumbs. Taste the three foods with eyes closed. Draw the thumbs in the table. Say what you found.

experiments.record: Draw the results table with a thumb in every box: up, sideways or down.

flow.do: 1. Get at least 3 people together, the more the better. 2. Draw a table: names down the side, and a picture of jaggery, a lime and a karela across the top. 3. Put each food on its own steel plate.
flow.say: We are going to find out if everyone likes the same tastes. Here are three foods. Let's make a table for what we find.
flow.kid: Help draw the table. Draw a jaggery, a lime and a karela at the top.
flow.parent: Three people is the least. Grandparents, older cousins or a neighbour make the test more interesting, because the ages are different.

flow.do: Point to each person and each food. Ask your child to guess the thumb, and to say why. Write the guesses in pencil on a separate paper.
flow.say: Will this person like the karela? Will that person like the lime? Thumbs up, sideways or down? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Will each person like each food? Why?

good: A grown-up will like karela, because they cook it a lot.
Everyone will like jaggery, because jaggery is sweet.

flow.do: 1. Hand everyone a piece of jaggery. 2. Everyone closes their eyes, tastes and chews. 3. Count 'one, two, three'. 4. Everyone opens their eyes and shows a thumb at the same time. 5. Everyone sips water. 6. Do the same with the lime, then the karela.
flow.say: Close your eyes and taste. Don't make a face yet! One, two, three: show your thumb.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Taste. On three, show your thumb.
flow.parent: Tasting with eyes closed, and showing thumbs together, stops people copying each other. Karela is safe raw in a small slice, but it is very bitter: a child can spit it out. A sip of water clears the mouth between foods.

flow.do: Help your child draw each person's thumb in the right box of the table.
flow.say: What did this person show for the karela? Draw their thumb in that box.
flow.kid: Draw each thumb in the right box.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child what they think, what they saw, and why. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Look at our table. Did everyone show the same thumb for the jaggery? And for the karela? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the table. Which food got the same thumbs? Which did not?

ask.q: Which food had the most thumbs up?
good: The jaggery.
Everyone liked the jaggery.

ask.q: We all ate the same karela. Why were the thumbs different?
good: Because karela tastes different to each person.
Because Paati is used to karela and I am not.

flow.parent: Most families find that nearly everyone likes the jaggery, and the thumbs are most different for karela and lime. If all the thumbs match, that is a real result too. Then ask each person: 'How bitter was the karela, a little or a lot?' The answers usually differ. A strong answer uses the table: 'We all ate the same karela, but the thumbs were different.'

check.q: Everyone ate the same karela, but the thumbs were different. What does this tell us?
options: Some people ate the wrong karela
The same food can taste different to different people
Thumbs are hard to show
check.why: Everyone ate the very same karela. So the difference was not in the food. It was in each person: their tongue, and the foods they are used to.

setup.art: Three small steel plates on a table: small lumps of jaggery, lime wedges and thin slices of karela, with glasses of water beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Put each food on its own plate.

setup.art: A family of four sitting round the table with eyes closed, each chewing a small piece of food.
setup.caption: 2. Everyone tastes with eyes closed.

setup.art: The same family holding up thumbs at the same moment: up, sideways and down, while a child draws them in a table.
setup.caption: 3. On three, everyone shows a thumb. Draw them in the table.

experiments.title: Who Said Hello? Can you tell people apart by voice alone?
experiments.context: In this experiment you close your eyes, and people at home say hello to you, one at a time. You guess who is talking. Then they whisper, and you guess again.
experiments.question: Can you tell who is talking just from their voice? Is it harder when they whisper?
experiments.predict: Guess first. How many people will you get right when they talk? When they whisper? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each person says the same words, 'Hello, how are you?', from the same spot across the room. Before you start, a grown-up writes the speakers' names on a paper in a mixed-up order, so the child cannot guess from the order. Everyone speaks in that order, then in a new mixed-up order for whispering.

materials.item: a dupatta or a soft cloth to cover the eyes, or just closed eyes
at least 2 people to speak (the grown-up and one more), or 1 person and a phone with a recorded voice of a relative
a sheet of paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Guess who is talking, with eyes closed. Then guess who is whispering. Tick the right guesses.

experiments.record: Draw a face for each person, and a tick or a cross under 'talking' and 'whispering'.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits on a chair with eyes closed or covered. 2. Everyone else stands across the room, quietly.
flow.say: Close your eyes. People will say hello. Guess who it is. How many do you think you will get right? Why?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Guess who says hello.

ask.q: How many will you get right? Why?
good: All of them, because I know everyone's voice.
Most of them, but two people sound alike.

flow.do: 1. Say the next name on the paper. 2. That person says 'Hello, how are you?' in a normal voice. 3. Your child guesses. 4. Mark a tick or a cross.
flow.say: Listen. Who is this?
flow.kid: Listen. Who is talking?

flow.do: Do the same again, but now everyone whispers. Use a new mixed-up order.
flow.say: Now everyone will whisper. Is it harder? Guess who it is.
flow.kid: Now they whisper. Who is it?
flow.parent: When we talk, a part of the throat called the voice box buzzes, and each person's buzz sounds a little different. When we whisper, the voice box does not buzz. So whispers sound more alike, and are harder to tell apart.

flow.do: Count the ticks for talking and for whispering. Ask the question below.
flow.say: How many did you get right when they talked? And when they whispered? Why was one harder?
flow.kid: Count your ticks. Which was harder?

good: Because whispers all sound the same.
Because a whisper has no buzz in it.

check.q: You could tell one person's voice from another's. What does this show?
options: Every person's voice is a little different
Everyone has the same voice
Only grown-ups have voices
check.why: Each person's voice is their own, so you can tell people apart without seeing them. Babies learn to know their mother's voice very early.

flow.parent: Whispers are usually harder to tell apart. If your child gets every one right both times, that is a real result too: they know these voices very well. Try again with a voice they hear less often, such as a neighbour.

setup.art: A boy sitting on a chair with a dupatta over his eyes, and three family members standing across the room.
setup.caption: 1. Close your eyes. People take turns to say hello.

setup.art: A woman whispering from across the room, with the boy tilting his head to listen.
setup.caption: 2. Now they whisper. Guess again.

activities.title: Mirror Twins: what is the same, what is different?
activities.context: In this activity you stand at a mirror with a grown-up or a brother or sister. You find ways you are similar, and ways you are different.

materials.item: a mirror, such as a dressing-table or bathroom mirror
paper and crayons

schedule.what: Look in the mirror together. Find 5 things that are the same and 3 that are different. Draw the two of you.

activities.record: Draw yourself and your mirror partner side by side. Circle one thing that is the same, and one that is different.

flow.do: 1. Stand side by side at the mirror. 2. Point to your eyes, then ask your child to point to theirs. 3. Do the same for ears, nose, mouth and hands.
flow.say: Look in the mirror. How many eyes do I have? How many do you have? Let's find five things that are the same.
flow.kid: Look in the mirror. Find five things that are the same.

ask.q: What is the same about us?
good: We both have two eyes and one nose.
We both have ten fingers and two ears.

flow.do: Now look closely together for things that are different.
flow.say: Now look closely. What is different about us?
flow.kid: Now find three things that are different.

good: You are taller.
Your hair is short and mine is long.
You have a mole on your cheek.

flow.parent: Good answers are about the body: height, hair, eyebrows, the shape of ears, a dimple, freckles or moles. Clothes count too, but help your child also find things that are part of them.

flow.do: Help your child draw the two of you. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Draw us both. Circle one thing that is the same, and one thing that is different.
flow.kid: Draw you and your partner. Circle a same thing and a different thing.

check.q: You and a grown-up both have two eyes. What is the word for this?
options: Similar
Different
Kind
check.why: Similar means alike in some way. Every person has two eyes, so you and the grown-up are similar there.

setup.art: A girl and her mother side by side at a bathroom mirror, both pointing at their eyes.
setup.caption: 1. Find five things that are the same.

setup.art: A child's drawing of two faces side by side, with the eyes circled in green and the hair circled in red.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the two of you. Circle a same and a different.

activities.title: All About Me: my name, my face, what I like
activities.context: In this activity you make a page all about you: a drawing of your face, your name and what it means, and three things you like.

materials.item: a sheet of paper
crayons or colour pencils
a small hand mirror, if you have one

schedule.what: Draw your face. Ask a grown-up what your name means. Draw three things you like.

activities.record: The 'All About Me' page. Keep it, and make a new one next year to see what has changed.

flow.do: 1. Give your child the paper and crayons. 2. Let them look in a mirror. 3. Ask them to draw their face in the middle of the page.
flow.say: Look at your face in the mirror. What colour are your eyes? What is your hair like? Draw yourself.
flow.kid: Look in the mirror. Draw your face in the middle.

flow.do: 1. Write your child's name at the top. 2. Tell them who chose the name, why, and what it means, if it has a meaning.
flow.say: I am writing your name at the top. Let me tell you who chose your name, and why. Do you know anyone else with your name?
flow.kid: Your name is on the top. Ask: who chose my name? What does it mean?
flow.parent: If you do not know the meaning, tell the story of how the name was chosen. Every child's name has a story.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw three things they like round the face: a food, a game and anything else.
flow.say: What is your favourite food? Your favourite game? Draw them round your face.
flow.kid: Draw three things you like round your face.

flow.do: Ask the question below.
flow.say: Would your best friend draw the same three things? Why or why not?
flow.kid: Would your friend draw the same things? Why?

ask.q: Would your friend like the same three things?
good: Maybe one, but not all three.
No, my friend likes cricket and I like drawing.

setup.art: A boy looking into a small hand mirror while drawing his own face on a sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 1. Look in the mirror and draw your face.

setup.art: A finished page with a child's face in the middle, the name at the top, and drawings of a dosa, a ball and a cat round the face.
setup.caption: 2. Add your name and three things you like.

activities.title: Favourite Fruit Tally: ask the family
activities.context: In this activity you ask people at home, and relatives on the phone, for their favourite fruit. You make a tally mark for each answer and find the most liked fruit.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a phone, to call grandparents, aunts or cousins

schedule.what: Ask 6 to 10 people their favourite fruit. Make a tally mark for each. Count the marks.

activities.record: The tally chart, with a drawing of each fruit and its tally marks.

flow.do: 1. Draw four fruits down the side of the paper: mango, banana, guava and 'other'. 2. Show your child how to make a tally mark, one line for each answer.
flow.say: We will ask people their favourite fruit. For each answer, you make one line next to that fruit.
flow.kid: Make one line for each answer, next to the right fruit.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess, and to say why.
flow.say: Which fruit do you think most people will choose? Why?
flow.kid: Guess. Which fruit will win? Why?

flow.do: 1. Your child asks each person at home. 2. Phone two or three relatives so your child can ask them too. 3. Your child makes a tally mark for each answer.
flow.say: Ask a relative on the phone: 'What is your favourite fruit?'
flow.kid: Ask: 'What is your favourite fruit?' Make a line.

flow.do: Count the lines for each fruit together.
flow.say: Count the lines. Which fruit has the most? Did everyone choose the same?
flow.kid: Count the lines. Which fruit has the most?

check.q: Not everyone chose the same fruit. What does this tell us?
options: Some people gave the wrong answer
People like different things
Only mango is a fruit
check.why: There is no wrong answer to 'What is your favourite fruit?'. People in one family can like different things.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a mango, a banana, a guava and a question mark drawn down the side, and tally lines next to each.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the fruits. Make a line for each answer.

setup.art: A girl holding a phone to her ear, asking a question, with the tally sheet on her lap.
setup.caption: 2. Ask people at home and on the phone.

activities.title: Feelings Faces: what is that person feeling?
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up makes faces for different feelings, and you guess the feeling. Then you draw four feelings. Knowing how someone feels helps you be kind.

materials.item: paper and crayons

schedule.what: Guess the feeling from a face. Draw happy, sad, scared and angry faces.

activities.record: Four faces: happy, sad, scared and angry, with one thing that makes you feel each one.

flow.do: Make a happy face, then a sad, a scared and an angry face. Your child guesses each one.
flow.say: Look at my face. How am I feeling? How can you tell?
flow.kid: Look at the face. What is the feeling?

ask.q: How can you tell I am sad?
good: Your mouth is turned down.
Your eyes look droopy.

flow.do: Your child draws four faces and says one thing that makes them feel each way.
flow.say: Draw a happy face. What makes you happy? Now draw a scared face. What makes you scared?
flow.kid: Draw four faces: happy, sad, scared, angry. What makes you feel each one?
flow.parent: Different things make different people happy or scared. Thunder scares one child and thrills another. Let your child's answers be their own.

flow.do: Ask the question below.
flow.say: If you see your friend with a sad face, what could you do?
flow.kid: Your friend looks sad. What can you do?

ask.q: What can you do for a sad friend?
good: Ask them what happened.
Sit with them, or give them a hug.

setup.art: A grandmother making an exaggerated surprised face while a small boy laughs and points.
setup.caption: 1. Guess the feeling from the face.

setup.art: A sheet with four simple faces drawn by a child: happy, sad, scared and angry.
setup.caption: 2. Draw four feelings.

projects.title: The Kindness Chain: one kind thing a day for a week
projects.context: In this week-long project you do one kind thing every day. For each one, you add a paper ring to a chain. At the end of the week, see how long your chain has grown.

materials.item: strips of coloured paper or old magazine pages, about two fingers wide
glue or tape
a crayon

schedule.what: Cut 7 strips. Do one kind thing. Draw it on a strip and make the first ring.
Do a kind thing. Add a ring.
Do a kind thing. Add a ring.
Do a kind thing for someone outside the family, or for an animal. Add a ring.
Do a kind thing. Add a ring.
Do a kind thing. Add a ring.
Add the last ring. Hang up the chain. Talk about which kind thing felt best.

projects.record: The paper chain, with a drawing of the kind thing on each ring.

flow.do: 1. Cut 7 paper strips together. 2. Ask your child for one kind thing they did today. 3. They draw it on a strip. 4. Glue the strip into a ring.
flow.say: What kind thing did you do today? Draw it on this strip. Then we make it into a ring.
flow.kid: Draw your kind thing on a strip. Make it into a ring.
flow.parent: A grown-up helps with the scissors. Small things count: holding a door, sharing a snack, saying sorry.

flow.do: Each day, your child adds a ring through the last one, with a drawing of the day's kind thing.
flow.say: What kind thing did you do today? Add a ring to the chain.
flow.kid: Draw today's kind thing. Add a ring.
flow.wait: Do one kind thing a day for 5 more days.
flow.parent: On one day, help your child be kind to someone outside the home, or to an animal: a bowl of water for the birds, or a drawing for the watchman.

flow.do: Hang up the chain. Count the rings together and ask the questions below.
flow.say: Look how long it is! Which kind thing made someone smile the most?
flow.kid: Count the rings. Which kind thing was the best?

ask.q: How did you feel when you were kind?
good: Happy.
Warm inside.

ask.q: How did the other person feel?
good: They smiled.
Paati said thank you.

setup.art: Seven strips of coloured paper and a glue stick on a table, with a child drawing a small picture on one strip.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a kind thing on a strip.

setup.art: A paper chain of seven rings hanging across a window, each ring with a small drawing.
setup.caption: 2. Add a ring each day. Hang up the chain.

challenges.title: A Party Plate for Everyone
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge. You plan a snack plate for a family get-together, so that every person finds something they like.
challenges.problem: Your family is coming over. People like different tastes. Can you plan one plate of snacks so that every person finds at least one thing they like?
constraints: Use only foods that are in your kitchen or easy to get.
Every person must have at least one thing they like.
materials: the taste test table from the experiment, if you did it
general: Put one sweet, one sour and one salty snack on the plate.
Ask everyone first what they like, then choose.
Use the taste test table to see who liked sweet and who liked sour.
creative: Make little name flags for each person, next to a snack they like.
Put a sweet and a sour dip side by side, so each person can choose.
Add one new food that nobody has tried, for the brave tasters.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your party plate. Then show it to someone at home and ask: 'Is there something here you would like?'

flow.do: Read the challenge to your child. Look at the taste test table together, if you did it.
flow.say: Your family is coming over. Everyone likes different things. How can we make one plate that has something for everyone?
flow.kid: Plan a snack plate. Everyone must find something they like.

flow.do: Your child asks two or three people what snacks they like.
flow.say: Go and ask two people at home what snack they like best.
flow.kid: Ask people: 'What snack do you like?'

flow.do: Your child draws a big plate and draws the snacks on it. Help with names if needed.
flow.say: Draw a big round plate. What will you put on it? Who is each snack for?
flow.kid: Draw your plate. Draw the snacks. Who is each one for?

flow.do: Check the plate together, person by person.
flow.say: Let's check. Is there something here for each person?
flow.kid: Check: is there something for everyone?

check.q: One guest loves sour things and another guest loves sweet things. What plate will make both happy?
options: A plate with only laddoos
A plate with laddoos and lime pickle
A plate with only lime pickle
check.why: People like different tastes. A plate with a sweet thing and a sour thing gives each of them something they like.

setup.art: A child asking her grandmother a question, holding a sheet of paper with a big circle drawn on it.
setup.caption: 1. Ask people what they like.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a round plate with laddoos, murukku, cucumber slices and lime pickle, with small name flags.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a plate with something for everyone.

items.p: Draw yourself and one person from your home, side by side. Circle one thing that is the same about you.
items.a: Two people, with a circle round something they share, such as two eyes or ten fingers.
items.why: A strong drawing circles a body part both people have. All people share the same body parts.
items.art: A blank box split into two halves.

items.p: Draw a line from each food to its taste.
items.why: Sweet, sour, salty and bitter are four of our tastes. Jaggery is sweet, lime is sour, karela is bitter and salt is salty.
items.art: A lump of jaggery, half a lime, a karela and a heap of salt on the left, and the four taste words on the right, mixed up.

items.p: Every person has a heart beating inside them.
items.why: True. Every person has a heart. This is one way all people are similar.

items.p: Everyone in the world likes mangoes.
items.why: False. Many people love mangoes, but not everyone. People like different things.

items.p: Is it the same for everyone, or different for each person? Circle the same things in green and the different things in red.
items.why: All people have a nose and need sleep and food. Favourite colours, voices and heights are different from person to person.

items.p: Three of these are things every person needs to live. Which one is not?
items.why: Every person needs air, water and food to live. A toy car is fun, but nobody needs one to live.

items.p: In the story, Nila, her father and her grandmother all showed thumbs up for one food. Which one?
items.why: All three of them gave the jaggery a thumbs up. Sweet is a taste nearly everyone likes. The pavakkai got three different thumbs.

items.p: Draw one kind thing you can do for someone at home today.
items.a: Any kind act, such as carrying a bag, sharing a snack or giving a hug.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the child helping another person or making them feel better.
items.art: A blank box with a small heart in one corner.

items.p: Look at the picture of six children. Count the children with curly hair.
items.why: Two of the six children have curly hair, and four have straight hair. Hair is one way people are different.
items.art: Six children standing in a row: the second and fifth have curly hair, the others straight hair.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: name two ways you and your best friend are different.
items.a: My friend is taller than me. My friend likes cricket and I like drawing.
items.why: A strong answer gives two real differences, such as how they look and what they like.

items.p: Lakshmi and her brother Arun are eating dinner in Madurai. Karela is on the table.

views.says: Karela is yucky. Nobody should eat karela.
I like karela. Arun just likes different tastes from me.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing Arun has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Lakshmi: the same karela tastes different to different people, so neither of them is wrong. Arun is right that karela is very bitter, and for him it really does taste yucky.
items.why: Many children think that if they dislike a food, the food is bad for everyone. The taste test shows the same food can taste different in each mouth.

items.p: Here are four faces. Label each one: happy, sad, scared or angry.
labels: face with a turned-down mouth and a tear
face with wide eyes and an open mouth
face with eyebrows pulled down and a tight mouth
items.why: Faces show how people feel. Knowing how someone feels helps us know how to be kind to them.
items.art: Four simple faces in a row with an empty label under each.

items.p: With your eyes closed, you can tell one grown-up's voice from another's.
items.why: True. Each person's voice is a little different, so we can tell people apart just by listening.

items.p: Paati gave karela a thumbs up, and you gave a thumbs down. You both ate the same karela. Say why, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: Karela tastes different to Paati and to me. Paati has eaten karela for many years, and her tongue is different from mine.
items.why: A strong answer says the food was the same, so the difference is in each person: their tongue and the foods they are used to.

items.p: In the taste test, why did everyone taste with their eyes closed?
opts: So nobody copies someone else's face
items.why: If people see each other's faces, they may copy them. With eyes closed, each person shows what they really think.

items.p: Put the taste test steps in the right order.
items: Draw the thumbs in the table
a: Draw the thumbs in the table
items.why: A scientist guesses first, then tests, then writes down what happened. The guess comes before the test, so the test can show if the guess was right.

items.p: Shreya lives in Pune. Her new friend Ritu has just moved there from Kolkata.

views.says: Ritu looks different from me and talks differently, so she must be very different inside.
Inside, we both have a heart, lungs and bones, and we both like to play. We are very similar.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing Shreya has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Ritu: all people have the same parts inside and the same needs. Shreya is right that Ritu looks and talks a little differently on the outside.
items.why: People often think that looking different means being different inside. Inside, all people share the same body parts and almost all the same genes.

items.p: In the voice test, why were whispers harder to guess than talking?
opts: A whisper has no buzz from the voice box, so voices sound more alike
People change their names when they whisper
items.why: When we talk, the voice box in our throat buzzes, and each person's buzz is a little different. A whisper is only breath, so whispers sound more alike.

items.p: Babies only a few hours old already like sweet tastes.
items.why: True. Scientists have seen new babies relax at a drop of sweet water and screw up their faces at bitter. We are born liking sweet.

items.p: Only people are kind to each other.
items.why: False. Elephants soothe other elephants who are upset. In tests, rats free other rats who are shut in. Many animals help each other.

items.p: Draw a snack plate with something on it for every person at home. Write or say who each snack is for.
items.a: A plate with several different snacks and a name next to each.
items.why: A strong plate has different tastes, sweet, sour and salty, so that each person finds something they like.
items.art: A large empty circle for a plate.

items.p: Sort these into two groups: things all people share, and things that are only yours.
items.why: All people have bones, need water and laugh. Your fingerprints are yours alone, and so are your favourite colour and song.

items.p: In the story, Kavya said 'Yuck' about Bornali's sour fish curry. What would have been a kind thing to say?
opts: 'What is it called? Can I smell it?'
items.why: Asking about Bornali's food is kind. It shows Kavya wants to know her. Saying 'Yuck' made Bornali feel sad.

items.p: Ask a grown-up: is there a food you did not like as a child, but like now? Say what they told you, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: Amma did not like coffee as a child, but she likes coffee now.
items.why: A strong answer reports a real food. Many people learn to like bitter or sour foods as they grow and eat them again and again.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a child. Label the parts that every person has: eyes, ears, nose, mouth, hands.
items.why: Every person has these body parts. This is one of the ways all people are similar.
items.art: A simple drawing of a child with five empty label lines pointing to the eyes, ears, nose, mouth and hands.

items.p: In 1931, a scientist called Arthur Fox tasted nothing in a white powder. A man working next to him said the same powder was very bitter. What did this show?
opts: The friend was making it up
The same powder can taste different to different people
The powder had no taste for anyone
items.why: Fox gave the powder to many people. Some found it bitter, and some tasted nothing. The same thing can taste different to different people.

quiz.p: Which one is true for every person?
quiz.why: Every person needs food to live and grow. Hair and liking karela are different from person to person.

quiz.p: Riya and her brother Sai both have two ears. Riya is tall and Sai is short. Which is a way they are different?
quiz.why: Riya is tall and Sai is short, so their height is different. They are similar in having two ears and needing sleep.

quiz.p: Anu says mango is the best fruit. Her friend Joy says guava is the best. Who is right?
quiz.why: A favourite fruit is about what each person likes, so both can be right. People like different things.

quiz.p: In a taste test, Paati gave karela a thumbs up and Divya, aged 6, gave a thumbs down. They ate the same karela. Why were the thumbs different?
opts: The same food can taste different to different people
quiz.why: The karela was the same. Each person's tongue, and the foods they are used to, are different. So neither Paati nor Divya is wrong.
Karela is bitter. Some people find the bitter taste very strong, and others hardly mind it.

quiz.p: Which kind of food do nearly all people like, even new babies?
quiz.why: People are born liking sweet tastes. Bitter and sour foods get more mixed thumbs.

quiz.p: On her first day, a new girl sits alone at lunch. What is a kind thing to do?
opts: Sit with her and ask her name
quiz.why: Sitting with her and asking her name helps her feel welcome. Being kind means helping someone feel better.

quiz.p: Why is it kind to ask 'What do you like?' before giving someone a snack?
opts: Because everyone likes the same snack
quiz.why: People like different tastes. Asking first means you give them something they will enjoy.

quiz.p: Which other animals have scientists seen helping each other?
quiz.why: Elephants soothe other elephants who are upset, and rats free other rats who are shut in. People are animals too, and we help each other as well.

quiz.p: In the voice test, why are the speakers' names written in a mixed-up order?
opts: So the child cannot guess from the order
quiz.why: If people spoke in the same order each time, the child could guess from the order and not the voice. Mixing it up makes the test fair.

quiz.p: What does a scientist do before a test?
opts: Guesses what will happen, and says why
quiz.why: A scientist guesses first and gives a reason. Then the test shows if the guess was right.

videos.title: Newborn babies tasting sweet, sour and bitter
videos.why: Shows that babies only hours old relax at sweet and screw up their faces at bitter, before they have learned anything about food.
videos.check: Find a real clip from a study or a science programme, not acted, showing newborn faces to sweet and bitter tastes.

videos.title: Elephant Empathy | ScienceTake | The New York Times
videos.why: Shows kindness in other animals: elephants touching and calling to another elephant who is upset.
videos.check: Not yet watched by a person: watch it first.

videos.title: How Do We Taste our Food? | The Sense of Taste | What Are Taste Buds? | The Dr. Binocs Show
videos.why: Shows the bumps on the tongue up close and how taste buds sense sweet, sour, salty and bitter.
videos.check: Not yet watched by a person: watch it first.

applications: Cooks at a wedding or a festival make sweet, sour, salty and spicy dishes, so that every guest finds something they like.
Doctors and nurses know that people feel pain, taste and smell differently, so they ask each person how they feel.
Food scientists test new foods on many different people, because one person's taste is not everyone's.
Teachers learn each child's name and what they like, so every child feels welcome in class.
Police can identify people by their fingerprints, because no two people's are the same.

spotted.text: A banana-leaf meal at a wedding in Kerala, with sweet payasam, sour pickle, salty chips and bitter pavakka thoran side by side.
spotted.art: A banana leaf with many small heaps of food: payasam, pickle, banana chips and a green bitter gourd dish.

spotted.text: A school lunch break, where every child's tiffin has a different food from a different home.
spotted.art: A row of children sitting on a school bench, each with a different open tiffin.

spotted.text: A family photo from a festival like Onam, Eid or Durga Puja, where everyone has the same kind of face, but no two faces are alike.
spotted.art: A big family photo with grandparents, parents and children, all smiling, each face different.

spotted.text: A crow at the window cawing loudly when another crow is in trouble, and other crows flying in.
spotted.art: Several crows on a balcony railing, all cawing and looking at one crow on the ground.

spotted.text: A metro or bus seat marked for older people, people with babies and people who need help.
spotted.art: A seat in a metro coach with a sign showing an older person, a mother with a baby and a person on crutches.

open_questions.q: When two people taste the same mango, do they feel the same sweetness?
open_questions.why_open: Each person can only feel their own taste. Scientists can ask people how strong a taste is, but nobody can feel another person's taste directly.

open_questions.q: Why do some people grow to love bitter foods like karela and coffee?
open_questions.why_open: Eating a food again and again helps. But scientists are still finding out how much comes from what we eat and how much from the body we were born with.

open_questions.q: Why are people and other animals kind, even to strangers?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have many ideas. Kindness helps groups live together, and it feels good. But nobody fully knows how kindness began.

ask_kids: What is one way you and a grown-up at home are similar? One way you are different?
Is there a food you did not like before, but like now?
Who in our family has a voice you could know with your eyes closed?
What kind thing did someone do for you today? How did it feel?
If a crow could tell you their favourite food, what do you think it would be?
What would be boring if everyone in the world were exactly the same?

jokes.j: Why did the karela go to school?
jokes.a: To become a little less bitter about maths!

jokes.j: What did one twin say to the other in the mirror?
Why did the jaggery get so many friends?
jokes.a: Because the jaggery was so sweet to everyone!

jokes.j: What did the lime say when someone pulled a face?
jokes.a: Sorry, I'm feeling a bit sour today!

jokes.j: Why do your fingertips never get lost?
jokes.a: Because their lines are like no one else's!

jokes.j: What do you call a whisper that wants to be heard?
Why did the elephant hug her friend?
jokes.a: Because a trunk hug is the biggest hug of all!

jokes.j: Why did the mango go to the doctor?
jokes.a: Because it was not peeling well!

jokes.j: What do you call a crow who tells jokes?

maths.problem: In a favourite fruit tally, 4 people chose mango, 2 chose banana and 3 chose guava. Which fruit was chosen most?
maths.explain: 4 is more than 3, and 3 is more than 2. So mango was chosen most. But 5 people chose banana or guava, so not everyone likes mango best.
maths.context: This is about the fruit tally, where you asked people their favourite fruit and made a line for each answer.
maths.why_maths: A tally shows at a glance how many people like each thing, and that a family does not all like the same.

maths.problem: In the taste test, 5 people tasted the jaggery. 5 gave thumbs up. Then 5 people tasted the karela, and only 2 gave thumbs up. How many fewer thumbs up did the karela get?
maths.explain: Start at 2 and count on to 5: 3, 4, 5. That is 3. The karela got 3 fewer thumbs up than the jaggery. Sweet tastes are liked by almost everyone, and bitter ones are not.
maths.context: This is about the taste test, where everyone tasted jaggery, lime and karela with eyes closed and showed a thumb.
maths.why_maths: Taking one number from another shows how much more people agreed about the sweet food than the bitter one.

maths.problem: Meera, aged 6, had 3 people at home for the voice test. She guessed all 3 right when they talked, and 1 right when they whispered. Which way was harder? Guess what might happen with 6 people.
maths.answer: Whispering was harder. With 6 people she would probably get fewer right when they whisper.
maths.explain: 3 right is more than 1 right, so talking was easier. With more people there are more voices to mix up.
maths.context: This is about the voice test, where you guessed who said hello with your eyes closed.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two numbers tells us which test was harder, and helps us predict a new test.

science: Arthur L. Fox, 'The relationship between chemical constitution and taste', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 18 (1932): phenylthiocarbamide (PTC) tasted bitter to some people and tasteless to others; first noticed in 1931.
Linda Bartoshuk and colleagues, 1990s: some people (supertasters) find bitter compounds such as PROP far more bitter than most.
Jacob Steiner, 1970s: the gustofacial reflex, newborns relax at sweet and grimace at bitter tastes.

Julie Mennella, Coren Jagnow and Gary Beauchamp, 'Prenatal and postnatal flavor learning by human infants', Pediatrics 107 (2001): babies whose mothers drank carrot juice in pregnancy liked carrot-flavoured cereal more.
Inbal Ben-Ami Bartal, Jean Decety and Peggy Mason, 'Empathy and pro-social behavior in rats', Science 334 (2011).
Joshua Plotnik and Frans de Waal, 'Asian elephants (Elephas maximus) reassure others in distress', PeerJ (2014).
Whispering uses breath without vibration of the vocal folds, which removes much of what makes voices recognisable. Speaker recognition from whispers is less accurate than from normal speech.
Fingerprints: no two people, including identical twins, have been found to share the same prints.
Cambridge Primary Science Stage 1, Unit 3 'Ourselves': 3.1 We are similar, 3.2 We are different (the mirror activity and the family tally).

roots.context: We have found ways we are like other people, and ways we are not. Now we ask what the taste test tells us about ourselves and others.

deep_truth.truth: Everyone at home ate the same jaggery and the same karela. Nearly everyone liked the jaggery. For the karela, the thumbs were different. So a taste happens where a food meets a tongue, and every tongue is a little different.
deep_truth.habit: We think a food has one taste that everyone gets. So when someone says 'yuck' to a food we love, we think they are wrong. The test shows each person meets the same food in their own way.
deep_truth.evidence: In the taste test, everyone ate pieces of the same jaggery, lime and karela, with eyes closed. The jaggery got nearly all thumbs up. The karela and lime got different thumbs from different people.

three.who_am_i: You are a person like every other person, with the same body parts and the same needs. You are also the only one with your face, your voice and your tastes.
three.what_is_life: Every living being senses the world in their own way. A tongue, a nose and an ear each meet the world and tell you about it.
three.what_is_this_world: People are not the only ones who help each other. Crows, elephants and rats do too.

roots.thread: People share the same body parts and almost all the same genes, yet each of us looks, sounds and tastes in our own way. Everything is conscious, and every being feels the world from where they are. So when we want to know what another person feels, we ask them instead of guessing.

teachings.source: Karaniya Metta Sutta (Sutta Nipata 1.8), a Buddhist teaching
teachings.teaching: Just as a mother would protect her only child with her life, let your heart be kind to all beings, without limit.
teachings.link: Kindness here is not only for people who are like us. It is for every being, however different they look or feel.

teachings.teaching: What use is wisdom to someone who will not treat another's pain as their own, and try to stop it?
teachings.link: In the Feelings Faces activity, you learned to see how someone else feels. The Tirukkural, from Tamil Nadu, says that knowing things is of little use without caring about other people's pain.
People help each other, and so do elephants and rats. This Jain teaching says that helping each other is what living beings do.

science.text: The same substance can taste strongly bitter to one person and hardly bitter to another. This runs partly in families, and partly comes from what each person is used to eating.
Nobody can feel another person's taste directly. Whether two people feel the same sweetness from the same mango is still an open question.

other_view.view: People differ in how strongly they taste, but they mostly agree on which foods are sweet, sour, salty or bitter. For them, what we share is much bigger than our differences, and the differences are small.

practice.title: A slow taste
practice.say: Close your eyes. I will put a small piece of jaggery on your tongue. Don't chew yet. Just feel it. Is it sweet straight away, or slowly? Now chew slowly. Now think of someone at home eating the same jaggery. Are they tasting what you taste? We can only ask them.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Put a bit of jaggery on your tongue. Don't chew. Feel the sweet come. Now chew slowly. Does someone else taste the same?

playtest: Walked through every game, experiment, activity, project and sheet as a parent and child in a city flat would, reading aloud. Games: both printables list every card (20 and 12); the 'ten toes' card did not fit the Everyone/Some piles, so it is now 'a mouth'; kindness cards no longer assume a brother, sister or Paati; both games work with 2 players. Taste test: steps and minutes agree (25), steps no longer name made-up people, and the sheet question now asks about the story, not a result the family may not get. Voice test: the speaker order is now written on paper by a grown-up, so it works with 2 speakers or a recorded voice, and minutes agree (15). Cut two repeated worksheet items from each sheet, replaced a joke that was not funny, fixed a Fox story mismatch, and removed repeated mango questions and 'Amma/Paati/Appa' from family-facing steps.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1931, Arthur Fox, a chemist in the USA, was pouring a white powder into a bottle. Some of the powder flew up into the air. The man working next to him said the dust tasted very bitter. Fox was surprised. He tasted nothing at all, even when he put some powder on his tongue. Until then, most people thought a food or a chemical tastes the same to everyone. Fox gave the powder to his friends and family. Some found it horribly bitter. Others tasted nothing. Other scientists tested many families, and found that tasting this powder runs in families, like the shape of your nose. In the 1990s, Linda Bartoshuk, an American taste scientist, found that some people taste bitter things much more strongly than most. She called them supertasters. So when your family makes different faces at karela, they may really be tasting it differently.
how_we_found_out.who: Arthur Fox, a chemist in the USA, and later Linda Bartoshuk, an American taste scientist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a food or a chemical tastes the same to every person.
